newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia proposes cutting 1997 budget by one fifth.
newsitem.headline: Russia proposes cutting 1997 budget by one fifth.

text.p: The Russian government has sent a bill to parliament that would cut spending of the underfunded 1997 budget by one-fifth and could foster one of the year's hottest political battles.

Mikhail Zadornov, head of the State Duma's budget committee, confirmed on Monday he had received the bill, which a government official said proposed 108 trillion roubles ($18.8 billion) in cuts to the 530-trillion-rouble budget.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is expected to go to the State Duma lower house himself on May 21 to defend the bill which the opposition Communist Party, the largest single group in the chamber, has vowed to resist.

"By all accounts, Viktor Chernomyrdin himself will present the document in the Duma on May 21," First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov, who is in charge of the budget cut plan, told Interfax news agency.

Government officials say the cuts, known as a sequester, reflect the reality of Russia's financial morass -- in which first quarter spending was 63 percent of planned levels on income of 57 percent -- rather than essentially new cuts which would inflict new pain.
"Cuts on paper do not mean cuts in fact," said Petrov, calculating that real outlays in the last three-quarters of the year would be higher than those in the first quarter.
But Zadornov said the communist-dominated Duma, which passed the 1997 budget only after months of contention in February, could hit back with a plan to print money.
"I do not rule out that the left part of the Duma will offer a bill on printing money in response to the sequester bill," he told Reuters. "I know such bills are being prepared."

He said the budget committee could take up the bill on May 13 or 14. Under the 1997 budget law, the government must present a sequestration bill if revenues in any quarter are less than 90 percent of plan.
Russia brought inflation down to 16.7 percent in the year to March from 79 percent a year earlier, thanks to tight controls on monetary policy.
President Boris Yeltsin and top officials have vowed not to turn on the presses -- a monetary solution used in the early days of economic reform.

Zadornov said the bill proposed cuts of 55 percent on supports to agriculture, some investment programmes and some social spending. Supports for the coal industry, military complexes and equipment purchases would be cut by 30 percent.

He said key social supports -- so-called protected areas of spending -- were generally not targeted by the proposed cuts, although the government proposed stripping some educational and investment programmes of their protected status.
The communists who allowed the unrealistic budget setting revenues of 434 trillion roubles to pass, have already said they will not accept the government's new plan.

"Do they really think the Duma will approve a sequestration of 100 trillion roubles?" Duma speaker Gennady Selezyov, a communist, said recently. "That will never pass, because it ruins the entire budget...we voted for."

The budget gap has been a chief concern of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which has suspended payments of a $10 billion three-year loan because of low tax revenues, although officials have said they expect payment to resume this month.
Yeltsin has repeatedly supported the young reformers, lauded by the IMF, who penned the plan and were promoted to top posts in a government reshuffle last month.
Yeltsin governs largely by decree and often vetoes anti-reform laws passed by the Duma. But his supporters are outnumbered in the lower house which often and vocally calls for increased spending.
